questions.q: What is Project 2's core requirement, as scoped in this kickoff?
options: Consolidate three separate legacy systems (orders, customers, inventory) into one Fabric Data Warehouse for cross-source BI reporting, without a big-bang cutover
Build a brand-new real-time dashboard with no existing systems involved
Replace the Fabric Data Warehouse with three separate lakehouses
Migrate a single source system to a faster version of itself
questions.explain: The three sources are a legacy SQL Server database, a cloud CRM, and a third-party inventory system, all consolidating into one warehouse.

questions.q: Why does Project 2 choose a Fabric Data Warehouse as its target, rather than a lakehouse like Project 1 used?
options: The BI team's cross-source reporting needs full T-SQL support and strong multi-table joins, which matches the warehouse's strengths better than a lakehouse's simple-aggregation case
Lakehouses cannot store historical data at all
Fabric Data Warehouses are always the correct choice regardless of query pattern
The choice was arbitrary and has no connection to the BI team's actual needs
questions.explain: Fabric Lesson 10's warehouse strengths and Lesson 11's lakehouse-vs-warehouse framework both point toward the warehouse for this query pattern.

questions.q: Why isn't this project's real processing-model question a batch-vs-streaming decision, unlike Project 1's?
options: All three legacy sources are batch-extractable, so the real design question is migration order and coexistence between old and new systems, not batch vs. streaming
Project 2 actually does require a streaming architecture identical to Project 1's
Processing model doesn't matter for migration projects
The three source systems produce continuous real-time event streams
questions.explain: Since all sources are batch-extractable, the interesting design question shifts to how migration order and coexistence are handled, which Lesson 71 addresses directly.

questions.q: What does "no big-bang cutover" require of this project's design, according to the kickoff?
options: The legacy systems must keep running during migration, with both the old systems and the new warehouse staying correct at the same time during an overlap period
All three legacy systems must be shut down immediately once migration begins
The warehouse must be built without any reconciliation against the old systems
Cutover must happen instantly with zero planning
questions.explain: The non-functional requirements explicitly state legacy systems keep running during migration, with minimal, scheduled downtime only at the eventual cutover.

questions.q: How does this kickoff apply the same process Project 1 used, even though the two projects have different shapes?
options: It reuses Lesson 2's functional/non-functional split and Lesson 4's storage-choice framework — the same process, answering different questions because the constraints differ
It invents an entirely new, unrelated process specific to migrations
It skips requirements gathering because the legacy systems already define requirements
It applies Lesson 6's Lambda architecture unchanged from Project 1
questions.explain: Chapter 1's system-design process is reused deliberately — the questions are the same, but migration-specific constraints (coexistence, reconciliation) produce different answers.
